label: Person
name: Adam Frederick of Seinsheim
summary:
Adam Friedrich von Seinsheim (1708–1779) was Prince-Bishop of Würzburg (1755–1779) and Prince-Bishop of Bamberg (from 1757), making him one of the most powerful ecclesiastical princes in the Holy Roman Empire and a significant patron of late Baroque and early Rococo art and architecture. His tenure as prince-bishop coincided with the greatest flowering of Balthasar Neumann's architectural legacy.

Adam Friedrich was the quintessential prince-bishop of the German Baroque: enormously wealthy, culturally ambitious, and exercising both temporal and spiritual power over his territories. His patronage of the arts included completion of Neumann's famous Würzburg Residence — one of the greatest Baroque palaces in Europe, with Tiepolo's ceiling frescoes in the Imperial Hall and the grand staircase. He also undertook significant building projects in Bamberg.

His rule coincided with the Seven Years' War (1756–1763), during which his territories suffered occupation. His post-war reconstruction and cultural patronage contributed to the late flourishing of German prince-episcopal culture before the Imperial Recess of 1803 abolished most of the ecclesiastical principalities. He represents the last great age of German Baroque cultural patronage under ecclesiastical princes.
